items.statement: The prevalence of a working carbon monoxide alarm in homes with a fuel-burning appliance is at least 10 percentage points lower in privately rented than in owner-occupied homes in the county.
items.rationale: The need is high after two deaths and a board decision about targeting; novelty is modest because the gap is reported elsewhere (claim c1) but not locally; feasibility depends on door-to-door response.
items.risks: Nonresponse among renters, tenure misreported at the door, and too few renters sampled.

items.statement: Homes heated mainly with solid fuel or bottled gas have a lower prevalence of working carbon monoxide alarms than homes heated with oil or heat pumps.
items.rationale: Heating type drives both risk and alarm need, and the retrieved case series points to these fuels.
items.risks: Heating type overlaps with tenure and rurality, so the two contrasts are not independent.

items.statement: Self-reported ownership overstates working carbon monoxide alarms by at least 20 percentage points.
items.rationale: Matters for any future telephone monitoring of the programme (claim c2).
items.risks: Respondents may test the alarm themselves before answering once the visit starts.

summary: Three hypotheses; h1 selected because it answers the targeting question directly.
